key_terms.meaning: Resistance of a fluid to shear flow; dynamic viscosity μ = shear stress ÷ velocity gradient, in Pa·s (N·s/m²), and kinematic viscosity ν = μ/ρ in m²/s or cSt.
A number showing how little an oil's viscosity changes with temperature; high VI means a flatter viscosity–temperature curve and steadier oil films.
The lowest temperature at which an oil gives off enough vapour to flash when a flame is passed over it; the fire-safety limit of the lubricant.
A semi-solid lubricant made of oil held in a soap or other thickener, used where oil cannot be retained or replenished often.
A sliding bearing in which a round shaft (the journal) turns inside a curved bush, carrying load through a fluid film.
A soft tin- or lead-based white-metal bearing alloy with low friction and good embeddability, poured as a thin lining on a steel bush.
The film is thinner than the surface roughness, so load is carried by a very thin film plus surface layers of lubricant; wear occurs but slowly.
A complete fluid film, thick enough to keep the surfaces fully apart, carries the load by pressure generated by the moving surface itself; no metal contact.
A rolling contact bearing using hardened steel balls as rolling elements; low friction, mainly radial and moderate axial load.
A rolling bearing with cylindrical rollers in line contact; high radial capacity; the plain type takes no axial load.
A roller bearing whose rollers are long and thin (diameter small compared with length); used where radial space is limited.
Partly boundary and partly hydrodynamic; a few high spots touch while other areas are supported on fluid.
ε = e/c, the shaft centre offset e divided by radial clearance c; h₀ = c(1 − ε) is the minimum film thickness.
The thinnest oil gap in a loaded journal bearing; the design must keep it larger than the combined surface roughness.
S = (r/c)² × (μn/p), with r journal radius, c radial clearance, μ viscosity in Pa·s, n speed in rev/s, p = W/(LD) projected bearing pressure in Pa.
Ratio of bearing length to journal diameter; low values leak oil at the ends, high values run hotter and misalign more.
The constant radial load at which 90% of a group of bearings reaches 1 million revolutions; the load capacity used in life calculation.
The static load that leaves a permanent deformation of 0.0001 × rolling-element diameter at the most heavily loaded contact; the load capacity for non-rotating or very slow bearings.

P = X F<sub>r</sub> + Y F<sub>a</sub>, with F<sub>r</sub> radial load, F<sub>a</sub> axial load, X and Y load factors from the bearing catalogue; it converts combined loading to one radial-equivalent value.

The life in revolutions (or hours) that 90% of identical bearings reach or exceed under a given load; L₁₀ = (C/P)<sup>p</sup> million revolutions, p = 3 for ball bearings and 10/3 for roller bearings.
For each L/D, ε, h₀/c, φ, (r/c)f, Q/(rcnL), Q<sub>s</sub>/Q and p/p<sub>max</sub> against S; for L/D = 1, S = 0.121 gives ε = 0.6 and (r/c)f = 3.22.
ΔT = 8.30 p (r/c)f / [Q/(rcnL)] °C with p in MPa, all friction heat carried by the oil flow.
C<sub>req</sub> = P L₁₀<sup>1/p</sup>, with L₁₀ = 60 n L<sub>10h</sub>/10⁶ million revolutions.
Seating W<sub>m2</sub> = π b G y; operating W<sub>m1</sub> = (π/4)G²p + 2π b G m p; the bolts carry the larger.
(d − h)/d, about 15 to 30 per cent for a static seal, with the groove filled under about 85 per cent.

takeaways: A lubricant does its job only if it stays between the surfaces, and viscosity is the property that decides whether it can.
Viscosity falls as oil gets hotter, so a lubrication design has to be checked at the running temperature, not the cold start.
Sliding bearings are quiet and cheap but need a full oil film; rolling bearings have low starting friction and need almost no attention.
In a journal bearing the shaft's own rotation drags oil into a wedge, and that converging gap is what builds the pressure that carries the load.
The Sommerfeld number collapses speed, viscosity, clearance and load into one number, which is why a single family of charts serves many bearings.
Raimondi and Boyd charts turn S and L/D into eccentricity, film thickness, friction and oil flow; a heat balance on that flow gives the temperature rise.
Bearing life falls steeply with load: life goes as (C/P)³ for ball bearings, so a 25% overload can halve or worse the life.
Bearing selection is a loop: guess a bearing, compute P, get required C, pick from the catalogue, then recheck C₀, speed limit and temperature.

Seals protect every bearing: gaskets and O-rings close static joints, lip seals, face seals and labyrinths close the gap round a shaft, and a gasket joint is bolted for the larger of its seating and operating loads.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the full chain in a long answer: Sommerfeld number, Raimondi and Boyd table reading, film thickness, friction, flow and temperature rise; or equivalent load, required rating and a catalogue choice with a static check. The exam course for this unit also asks for the design of seals and gaskets.

bank.q: Define viscosity and viscosity index. Explain why the same oil may be right for a machine in a Chennai summer and wrong in a cold hill station, and what the designer does about it.
outline: Dynamic viscosity μ = τ ÷ (du/dy) in Pa·s; kinematic viscosity ν = μ/ρ in m²/s or cSt
Viscosity falls steeply as temperature rises
Viscosity index as the flatness of the viscosity–temperature curve
Hot running sets the least viscosity that keeps the film; cold start sets the most that still flows
Remedies: high-VI or multigrade oil, warm-up, heater or cooler, thermostat

answer.text: Dynamic viscosity. A fluid sheared between a fixed plate and a moving plate develops a shear stress proportional to the velocity gradient: τ = μ du/dy. The constant μ is the dynamic viscosity, in Pa·s (N·s/m²). It is the property that sets the friction and the film pressure in a bearing.

Kinematic viscosity. ν = μ/ρ, in m²/s; oil data sheets quote it in centistokes, 1 cSt = 10⁻⁶ m²/s. Example: an oil with μ = 0.05 Pa·s and ρ = 900 kg/m³ has ν = 0.05/900 = 5.56 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s = 55.6 cSt. Standard viscometers time gravity flow, which is why ν is the catalogue value.

Effect of temperature. The viscosity of every oil falls steeply as it warms: a machine oil can lose most of its viscosity between a cold start and its running temperature. Too thin and the film breaks and metal touches; too thick and the oil will not reach the bearing and churning raises the temperature.

Viscosity index (VI). VI is a number that says how little the viscosity changes with temperature. A high VI means a flat viscosity–temperature curve. It does not mean a thick oil: two oils with the same 40 °C viscosity can have VI 95 and VI 150, and the second keeps more of its viscosity when hot and stiffens less when cold.

The Chennai machine. The machine runs hot, perhaps an ambient of 38 °C plus its own friction heat. The design point is the hot end: the viscosity at the running temperature must still keep the film thickness above the roughness. A fairly heavy grade is chosen, and cold starting is no problem.

The hill-station machine. The same heavy grade, started on a 5 °C morning, is so thick that it pours slowly (its pour point may be close), the pump struggles and the bearing runs starved for the first minutes, which is when most wear happens. In service the machine may never reach the temperature the grade was chosen for, so friction loss stays high.

What the designer does. (a) Choose a high-VI or multigrade oil (for example a 15W-40 type): it behaves like a thin oil when cold and a thicker one when hot. (b) Check the viscosity at both ends of the temperature range, not only at 40 °C. (c) Add a sump heater or a warm-up run for cold sites, or an oil cooler and thermostat for hot ones. (d) Check the pour point is well below the coldest start.

Closing check. A selection is correct when, at the hottest running temperature, the computed film thickness still meets the roughness rule, and at the coldest start the oil still pours and reaches the bearing within seconds.

bank.q: Compare sliding contact and rolling contact bearings under load capacity, friction, starting torque, space, noise, cost and maintenance. Place boundary, mixed and hydrodynamic lubrication on the same picture.
outline: Construction: journal and bush against rings, rolling elements and cage
Friction and starting torque
Load capacity for the space, shock, noise, cost, maintenance
Axial and radial space
Lubrication regimes with friction levels
Typical uses of each

answer.text: Construction. A sliding (plain) bearing is a journal turning in a bush of softer metal such as babbitt or bronze, separated by an oil film. A rolling bearing has an inner ring, an outer ring, balls or rollers and a cage; the load passes through rolling contacts.
Comparison.

head: Point
Sliding contact
Rolling contact
rows: about 0.002 to 0.01 with a full film; 0.05 to 0.15 at start
about 0.001 to 0.005, nearly the same at start
very high, and can be split round a crankshaft
needs a larger bearing; races may brinell
cheap shell, but oil system needed
often sealed with grease for life

answer.text: Friction with numbers. For d = 100 mm, W = 20 kN and 900 rpm (ω = 94.25 rad/s): a plain bearing with μ = 0.01 loses T ω = 0.01 × 20 000 × 0.05 × 94.25 = 942.5 W; a rolling bearing with μ = 0.002 loses 188.5 W.

The three regimes. Plot the friction coefficient of a plain bearing against the bearing modulus μN/p. At very small μN/p (start, very slow, very heavy load) the film is thinner than the roughness: boundary lubrication, μ about 0.05 to 0.15, and the surface layers of the oil and its additives protect the metal. As speed builds, part of the load rides on a film: mixed lubrication, friction falling steeply. Past the minimum of the curve the film is complete: hydrodynamic lubrication, μ about 0.002 to 0.01, rising slowly with μN/p as the oil is sheared more.

Where rolling bearings sit. A rolling bearing runs on a very thin elastohydrodynamic film squeezed between curved contacts, so its friction is low from the start and changes little with speed; it never passes through a high-friction start.

Uses. Sliding: crankshafts and connecting rods, steam and gas turbines, large slow machines with shock (rolling mills), split housings. Rolling: electric motors, fans, gearboxes, machine tool spindles, wheel hubs, anything that starts often under load.

Conclusion. Choose a sliding bearing for very heavy or shock load, very large shafts, quiet running or split assembly, when an oil supply is available. Choose a rolling bearing for low starting torque, short axial length, easy replacement and little maintenance.

bank.q: Explain how a hydrodynamic oil film is generated in a journal bearing. Define eccentricity ratio, minimum film thickness and attitude angle, and state the condition for full film lubrication.
outline: Journal drags oil into a converging wedge
Pressure rises in the converging part, falls and may cavitate in the diverging part; resultant balances the load
Journal centre takes an equilibrium offset e
ε = e/c, h₀ = c(1 − ε), attitude angle φ
Full film: h₀ well above combined roughness; needs speed, viscosity and supply

answer.text: Geometry. The journal of radius r turns in a bush of slightly larger radius; the difference is the radial clearance c, a fraction of a millimetre. Under load W the journal centre moves off the bush centre by the eccentricity e, so the gap is no longer uniform.

Wedge action. Oil sticks to the journal surface and is dragged round with it. On the side where the gap narrows in the direction of rotation, the oil is forced into a converging passage. To pass the same flow through a smaller section, the pressure must rise. This is the hydrodynamic wedge.

Pressure field. Pressure builds from the oil inlet, peaks a little before the minimum gap and falls back to ambient soon after it. In the diverging part the pressure would go below ambient, so the oil releases vapour and air (cavitation); that part carries almost no load. The resultant of the positive pressure balances W.

Equilibrium. The journal centre settles where the film force equals the load. It does not sit straight below the bush centre: it is displaced at an angle to the load line, in the direction of rotation.

Definitions. Eccentricity ratio ε = e/c (0 for a centred journal, 1 for metal contact). Minimum film thickness h₀ = c − e = c(1 − ε). Attitude angle φ is the angle between the load line and the line joining the two centres. Example: c = 0.05 mm and ε = 0.6 give e = 0.03 mm and h₀ = 0.02 mm = 20 μm.

Condition for a full film. The film is complete when h₀ exceeds the combined roughness of journal and bush plus the largest dirt particle the filter passes, with a margin. A widely used rule asks for h₀ ≥ 0.005 + 0.00004 D mm; for D = 50 mm that is 7 μm, so the 20 μm film above is safe.

What it needs. Enough speed (the film collapses at start and stop), enough viscosity at the running temperature, a continuous oil supply fed into the unloaded side, and no groove across the loaded arc, which would let the pressure escape.

Check. If speed doubles at the same load and oil, the Sommerfeld number doubles, ε falls and h₀ rises; if the oil heats and thins, the reverse happens. A design is therefore checked at the hottest running condition.

bank.q: Define basic dynamic load rating C and basic static load rating C₀ of a rolling bearing. Explain the physical meaning of each and when each governs the selection.
outline: C: load giving a rating life of one million revolutions with 90 % reliability
C₀: static load giving total permanent deformation 0.0001 × rolling-element diameter
C governs rotating service through L₁₀ = (C/P)<sup>p</sup>
C₀ governs stationary, very slow or shock-loaded bearings through s₀ = C₀/P₀
Both are catalogue values; check both and the limiting speed

answer.text: How rolling bearings fail. A bearing turning under load fails by fatigue: after many stress cycles a flake of raceway metal spalls out. A bearing standing still under heavy or shock load fails differently: the rolling elements press permanent dents into the races (brinelling). The two ratings cover the two failures.

Basic dynamic load rating C. The constant radial load (axial for a thrust bearing) under which a large group of identical bearings reaches a rating life of one million revolutions, with 90 % of them still running. It is a reference load, not a load the bearing should carry; real loads are far smaller.

Using C. The life at an equivalent load P is L₁₀ = (C/P)<sup>p</sup> million revolutions, p = 3 for ball and 10/3 for roller bearings. Example: C = 30 kN, P = 6 kN gives L₁₀ = 5³ = 125 million revolutions, which is 125 × 10⁶/(60 × 1500) = 1389 h at 1500 rpm.

Basic static load rating C₀. The static load that produces a total permanent deformation of 0.0001 of the rolling-element diameter at the most heavily loaded contact. Up to that dent the bearing still runs smoothly; beyond it the dents make it noisy and rough.

Using C₀. Find the equivalent static load P₀ (for a deep-groove ball bearing, the larger of F<sub>r</sub> and 0.6 F<sub>r</sub> + 0.5 F<sub>a</sub>) and require s₀ = C₀/P₀ of about 1.5 to 2 for quiet running, 2 to 3 for ordinary machinery and 3 or more with shock. C₀ also enters the deep-groove factors through F<sub>a</sub>/C₀.

When each governs. C governs a bearing that turns at normal speed for a stated life: a motor, fan or gearbox. C₀ governs a bearing that is stationary or oscillates slowly under heavy load, or sees shock at rest: a crane hook swivel, a slewing ring, a bridge bearing. A bearing must pass both checks, plus its limiting speed.

Closing check. In the selection example of the chapter on selection, bearing B passed on C (C<sub>req</sub> = 55.0 kN against 55.3 kN) and on C₀ (s₀ = 31.5/5 = 6.3), so the dynamic rating, not the static one, set the size.

bank.q: Classify seals used in machines. Describe a gasket, an O-ring, a lip seal, a mechanical face seal and a labyrinth seal, and state where each is used.
outline: Static against dynamic; contact against clearance
Gasket: seating stress y and gasket factor m
O-ring: squeeze and groove fill
Lip seal: lip and garter spring, faces the oil
Face seal: lapped faces, spring load
Labyrinth: no contact, small steady leak
Selection by motion, speed, pressure and leakage allowed

answer.text: Purpose. A seal keeps lubricant in and dirt, water or process fluid out. A bearing that loses its oil or takes in grit fails long before its rated life, so the seal is part of the bearing design.

Classification. Static seals close a joint between parts that do not move relative to each other: gaskets, O-rings in cover grooves, liquid sealants. Dynamic seals close the gap round a moving shaft or rod: lip seals, mechanical face seals, O-rings on slow rods, labyrinths, gland packing. Contact seals press a soft or lapped surface against the moving part; clearance seals leave a small gap and accept a small leak.

Gasket. A compressible ring clamped between flanges. It must first be crushed to its seating stress y to fill the flange roughness, and under pressure it must keep m times the fluid pressure. Used on pipe flanges, pump casings, engine heads and covers.

O-ring. A ring of round section squeezed in a groove, typically by 15 to 30 per cent of its section for a static seal, with the groove filled well under 85 per cent. Example: d = 3.53 mm in a 2.80 mm deep, 4.80 mm wide groove gives squeeze 21 % and fill 73 %. Used on covers, hydraulic cylinders and valves.

Lip seal. A rubber lip, held on the shaft by a garter spring, runs on a thin oil film; the lip faces the oil. A ground, hard shaft is needed. Used on gearbox, motor and axle shafts at moderate surface speed and low pressure.

Mechanical face seal. A spring presses a rotating carbon ring against a stationary silicon carbide or ceramic ring; the leak path is the micron gap between lapped faces. Used on pumps for water, fuel and chemicals.

Labyrinth seal. Fins with a small radial gap and no contact; each fin throttles the leak. No wear and no friction heat, so it suits steam turbines and compressors at high speed, but it always leaks a little.
Gland packing. Braided rings squeezed by a gland nut on valves and slow pumps; it is allowed to drip to stay cool.

Selection. Pick by motion (none, rotary, sliding), surface speed, pressure, temperature and how much leakage is allowed: gasket or O-ring for a cover, lip seal for an oil-bath gearbox shaft, face seal for a pump, labyrinth for a turbine.

bank.q: A journal of 60 mm diameter and 60 mm length runs at 1200 rpm with oil of μ = 0.020 Pa·s at the working temperature. Radial clearance is 0.06 mm and the load is 6 kN. Compute the bearing pressure and the Sommerfeld number, and from the L/D = 1 table find the eccentricity ratio and the minimum film thickness. Is the film thick enough?
outline: n = 20 rev/s, r/c = 500
p = W/(LD) = 1.67 MPa
Interpolate between S = 0.121 and 0.0446
h₀ = c(1 − ε), compare with 0.005 + 0.00004 D

answer.text: Projected area and pressure: L D = 0.06 × 0.06 = 3.6 × 10⁻³ m², so p = 6000/(3.6 × 10⁻³) = 1.667 × 10⁶ Pa = 1.67 MPa.
Clearance ratio: r/c = 0.03/(0.06 × 10⁻³) = 500, and (r/c)² = 250 000.
Sommerfeld number: μn/p = 0.020 × 20/(1.667 × 10⁶) = 2.4 × 10⁻⁷, so S = 2.4 × 10⁻⁷ × 250 000 = 0.060. It is dimensionless and inside the table range.
Table rows that bracket S = 0.060 (L/D = 1):
Minimum film thickness: h₀ = 0.240 × 0.06 = 0.0144 mm = 14.4 μm.
Film check: the roughness rule asks for h₀ ≥ 0.005 + 0.00004 × 60 = 0.0074 mm. The bearing gives 0.0144 mm, almost twice that, so the film is safe at this temperature.
Closing check: S = 0.060 lies between the two rows and ε = 0.76 lies between 0.6 and 0.8 in the same proportion, so the reading is consistent with the trend (smaller S, larger ε).

bank.q: A full journal bearing with L/D = 1 has d = L = 50 mm, c = 0.05 mm, W = 5 kN and N = 1500 rpm, with oil of μ = 0.0387 Pa·s at the film temperature. Find the Sommerfeld number, and from the Raimondi and Boyd table the eccentricity ratio, minimum film thickness, friction coefficient, friction power, oil flow, side leakage, peak film pressure and temperature rise.
outline: S = (μn/p)(r/c)² with n in rev/s and p = W/(LD)
S ≈ 0.121 is a table row: read ε, h₀/c, (r/c)f, Q/(rcnL), Q<sub>s</sub>/Q, p/p<sub>max</sub>
f = (r/c)f ÷ (r/c), T = fWr, P = 2πnT
Q = (flow variable) r c n L
ΔT from the heat balance
Check h₀ against the roughness rule

answer.text: Pressure: p = W/(LD) = 5000/(50 × 50) = 2.0 N/mm² = 2.0 MPa.
Table row for L/D = 1 at S = 0.121 (no interpolation needed):
Eccentricity and film: ε = 0.6, so h₀ = c(1 − ε) = 0.05 × 0.4 = 0.020 mm = 20 μm.
Oil flow: Q = 4.33 × r c n L = 4.33 × 25 × 0.05 × 25 × 50 = 6766 mm³/s = 6.77 cm³/s. Side leakage Q<sub>s</sub> = 0.680 × 6766 = 4601 mm³/s; the rest, 2165 mm³/s, leaves round the circumference.
Peak pressure: p<sub>max</sub> = p ÷ 0.415 = 2.0/0.415 = 4.82 MPa, well within what a babbitt or bronze lining carries.
Temperature rise, all friction heat into the flow: ΔT = 8.30 p (r/c)f / [Q/(rcnL)] = 8.30 × 2.0 × 3.22/4.33 = 12.3 °C. Check by energy: 126.4 W ÷ (860 × 1760 × 6.766 × 10⁻⁶) = 12.3 °C.
Film check: 0.005 + 0.00004 × 50 = 0.007 mm; h₀ = 0.020 mm is almost three times that, so the bearing runs with a safe full film.

Each chart reading explained: ε locates the journal; (r/c)f gives friction once divided by r/c; the flow variable sizes the oil supply; Q<sub>s</sub>/Q tells how much oil leaves the ends; p/p<sub>max</sub> gives the peak pressure for the lining. The table holds for a full 360° bearing with steady load and one mean viscosity.

bank.q: A deep-groove ball bearing carries a radial load of 5 kN at 900 rpm and must last 10 000 hours. Find the required basic dynamic load rating, and the life a bearing with C = 46.2 kN would give. Take p = 3.
outline: L₁₀ = 60 n L<sub>10h</sub>/10⁶ = 540 million revolutions
P = F<sub>r</sub> since there is no thrust
C<sub>req</sub> = P L₁₀<sup>1/3</sup> = 40.7 kN
Pick the next bearing with C ≥ C<sub>req</sub>; check C₀ and speed
Life of the chosen bearing

answer.text: Equivalent load: the bearing carries no axial load, so X = 1, Y = 0 and P = F<sub>r</sub> = 5 kN.
Life in million revolutions: L₁₀ = 60 n L<sub>10h</sub>/10⁶ = 60 × 900 × 10 000/10⁶ = 540.
Required rating: from L₁₀ = (C/P)³, C<sub>req</sub> = P × L₁₀<sup>1/3</sup> = 5 × 540<sup>1/3</sup> = 5 × 8.143 = 40.7 kN.
Choice: take the smallest bearing of the shaft bore with C ≥ 40.7 kN from the catalogue. A bearing with C = 46.2 kN qualifies.
Life of that bearing: L₁₀ = (46.2/5)³ = 9.24³ = 788.9 million revolutions; L<sub>10h</sub> = 788.9 × 10⁶/(60 × 900) = 14 609 h, comfortably above 10 000 h.
Static check: P₀ = F<sub>r</sub> = 5 kN; with s₀ = 2 the bearing needs C₀ ≥ 10 kN, which any bearing of this C easily has. Confirm the limiting speed is above 900 rpm for the chosen lubricant.
Units check: C and P both in kN, life in million revolutions inside the cube root. Putting 10 000 h directly would give 5 × 10 000<sup>1/3</sup> = 107.7 kN, a bearing 2.6 times too big.

bank.q: A deep-groove ball bearing carries F<sub>r</sub> = 4 kN and F<sub>a</sub> = 1.6 kN at 1200 rpm. For this bearing e = 0.28, X = 0.56 and Y = 1.5, and the load factor for the drive is 1.3. Find the equivalent dynamic load and the rating life in hours of a bearing with C = 35 kN.
outline: F<sub>a</sub>/F<sub>r</sub> = 0.4 > e, so X and Y apply
P = X F<sub>r</sub> + Y F<sub>a</sub> = 4640 N
Design load = 1.3 × 4640 = 6032 N
L₁₀ = (C/P)³ = 195 million revolutions
L<sub>10h</sub> ≈ 2713 h

answer.text: Which factors apply: F<sub>a</sub>/F<sub>r</sub> = 1.6/4 = 0.40, greater than e = 0.28, so X = 0.56 and Y = 1.5 (below e it would be X = 1, Y = 0).
Equivalent load: P = X F<sub>r</sub> + Y F<sub>a</sub> = 0.56 × 4000 + 1.5 × 1600 = 2240 + 2400 = 4640 N.
Load factor: the drive adds shock and vibration, so the design load is 1.3 × 4640 = 6032 N.
Life in revolutions: L₁₀ = (C/P)³ = (35 000/6032)³ = 5.802³ = 195.4 million revolutions.

Comment: about 2700 h is short for industrial machinery (often 8 000 to 20 000 h are asked). Because life goes as C³, a bearing with C = 50 kN would give (50 000/6032)³ = 569.6 million revolutions, or 7911 h.
Check: without the load factor the life would be (35 000/4640)³ = 429.2 million revolutions = 5961 h; the factor of 1.3 cuts life by 1.3³ = 2.2 times, as the numbers show (5961/2713 = 2.2).

bank.q: A flanged joint is sealed with a spiral-wound stainless steel gasket (m = 3.00, y = 69 MPa) of inside diameter 400 mm and outside diameter 430 mm. The design pressure is 3 MPa and the allowable bolt stress is 172 MPa. Find the effective gasket width, the diameter G, the seating and operating bolt loads, the bolt area, and choose the bolts.
outline: N = 15 mm, b₀ = 7.5 mm > 6.4 mm, so b = 2.5√b₀
G = outside contact diameter − 2b
W<sub>m2</sub> = π b G y; W<sub>m1</sub> = (π/4)G²p + 2π b G m p
Larger load governs; A<sub>m</sub> = W<sub>m</sub>/σ<sub>b</sub>
Number and size of bolts with stress areas

answer.text: Gasket width: N = (430 − 400)/2 = 15 mm, so the basic seating width b₀ = N/2 = 7.5 mm.
Effective width: b₀ is more than 6.4 mm, so b = 2.5√b₀ = 2.5 × √7.5 = 2.5 × 2.739 = 6.85 mm.
Reaction diameter: for a wide gasket G = outside contact diameter − 2b = 430 − 2 × 6.85 = 416.3 mm.
Seating load: W<sub>m2</sub> = π b G y = π × 6.85 × 416.3 × 69 = 617 850 N = 617.9 kN.
Operating load:
Governing load: W<sub>m2</sub> = 617.9 kN is larger than W<sub>m1</sub> = 569.5 kN, so here the seating of the hard spiral-wound gasket, not the pressure, sets the bolts.
Bolt area: A<sub>m</sub> = 617 850/172 = 3592 mm².
Bolt choice:
Choose 24 bolts of M16 (total 3768 mm² ≥ 3592 mm²): smaller bolts at a closer pitch load the gasket more evenly round a 416 mm circle. 16 bolts of M20 would also carry the load with fewer holes.

Check: the bolts at 172 MPa on 3768 mm² carry 648 kN, more than both 617.9 kN and 569.5 kN. With a soft compressed-fibre gasket (y = 11 MPa) the seating load would drop to about 98 kN and pressure would govern instead.

bank.q: Explain why the Sommerfeld number alone does not fix a journal bearing design, and how temperature rise, oil supply and L/D ratio are handled in the design loop.
outline: S needs μ, and μ depends on the film temperature the bearing itself creates
Friction heats the oil; viscosity falls; S falls; ε rises
Loop: assume temperature, μ, S, table, friction and flow, ΔT, compare
Separate curves for each L/D because of side leakage
Supply must replace the flow the table gives
Final checks on h₀ and temperature

answer.text: S is only the input. S = (μn/p)(r/c)² fixes the operating point on a chart only once μ is known, and μ is the viscosity at the mean film temperature, which is not known until friction and flow have been found. So S is part of a loop, not the end of the design.

The physical chain. Friction power heats the oil; hot oil is thinner; lower μ gives a smaller S; smaller S means larger ε and a thinner film; a thinner film can raise friction further. The design must find the temperature at which heat generated equals heat carried away.
The loop, step by step.

head: Step
Action
rows: Assume a mean film temperature, for example inlet + 10 °C
Read μ at that temperature from the oil chart
Compute S and enter the curve for the chosen L/D
New mean temperature = inlet + ΔT/2; if it differs from step 1, repeat

answer.text: A worked pass. For the bearing of the Raimondi and Boyd chapter (D = L = 50 mm, c = 0.05 mm, W = 10 kN, 25 rev/s, μ = 0.02 Pa·s) S = 0.03125, ε = 0.85, h₀ = 7.4 μm, friction 107 W, Q = 7.32 cm³/s and ΔT = 9.7 °C. If the oil enters at 40 °C the mean film is about 45 °C; if μ = 0.02 Pa·s was the 45 °C value, the loop has closed in one pass. If not, take μ at 45 °C and repeat.

Oil supply. The flow variable gives the oil the film itself pumps; the supply groove and pump must deliver at least that (7.3 cm³/s above), at the unloaded side. Too little supply starves the film and the chart answer no longer holds.

L/D. End leakage depends on length, so each L/D has its own curve. A short bearing (L/D = 0.5) leaks more oil and runs cooler but has a smaller S for the same load and runs more eccentric; a long one (L/D above 1) carries more load but is sensitive to shaft slope and runs hotter. L/D is chosen first and the loop is run for it; if h₀ fails, a longer bearing or a thicker oil is tried.

Final checks. When the loop converges, check h₀ against the roughness rule (7.4 μm against 7 μm above, a narrow pass), the outlet temperature against the oil limit, and the peak pressure against the lining.
Conclusion. S collapses four variables into one, but viscosity ties it to temperature, so a design is fixed only when S, ε, friction, flow and ΔT agree with each other at one temperature.

bank.q: A newly installed rolling bearing on a pump fails in three months instead of the expected three years. List the likely causes and explain how each one is detected and corrected.
outline: Load under-estimated: thrust, unbalance, belt pull
Wrong or lost lubricant
Contamination through a failed or missing seal
Misalignment and shaft deflection
Wrong fits
Mounting damage and false brinelling
Diagnosis from the raceway pattern, vibration and temperature

answer.text: Scale of the problem. Three months is about one twelfth of three years. Since life goes as (C/P)³, a load only 12<sup>1/3</sup> = 2.3 times the design value would explain it on its own, so load is the first suspect, but other causes are more common.

Under-estimated load. Thrust from an impeller, unbalance or a tight belt raises P. Detection: the spalled band runs round the raceway, wider than normal, offset to one side if thrust was missed. Correction: measure the real loads, recompute P = X F<sub>r</sub> + Y F<sub>a</sub> with the right factors, reselect.

Lubrication failure. Too little grease, the wrong grade, or grease washed out. Detection: discoloured (blue or brown) races, a glazed track, high running temperature. Correction: right grease and quantity, a relubrication interval, oil if the speed is high.

Contamination. Water or grit through a worn or missing seal. Detection: dents and scratches across the track, rust, gritty grease. Correction: a better seal, such as a lip seal facing outward against dirt, a labyrinth or a double-lip seal, and clean assembly.
Misalignment and shaft deflection. Detection: the wear track runs diagonally or sits at the edge of the race. Correction: align the pump and motor, stiffen the shaft, or use a self-aligning bearing.

Wrong fits. A fit too tight removes internal clearance and the bearing overheats; one too loose lets the ring creep and fret. Detection: heat at start, or polished bores and fretting rust. Correction: the catalogue fits for the load direction.

Mounting damage and false brinelling. Hammer blows through the rolling elements, or vibration while standing idle, dent the races at the ball pitch. Detection: evenly spaced dents. Correction: press fit through the right ring, and turn or isolate standby pumps.
Diagnosis method. Inspect the failed bearing first, since the track pattern points to the cause; then read the vibration spectrum and temperature records of the replacement.
Conclusion. Fix the cause before fitting a new bearing; otherwise the replacement fails in another three months.

bank.q: Discuss the effect of radial clearance c on the performance of a hydrodynamic journal bearing, using the bearing D = L = 50 mm, W = 10 kN, 1500 rpm, μ = 0.02 Pa·s with c = 0.04, 0.05 and 0.06 mm. Then discuss L/D and recommend a choice.
outline: S carries (r/c)², so c moves the operating point strongly
Compute S, ε, h₀, f, friction power, flow and ΔT for each c
Smaller c: higher S and thicker film here, but more heat per unit flow
Larger c: more flow and cooler, but more eccentric and thinner film
L/D effect
Recommendation with the roughness rule

answer.text: How c enters. S = (μn/p)(r/c)², so S varies as 1/c². Here μn/p = 0.02 × 25/(4 × 10⁶) = 1.25 × 10⁻⁷ for every case; only r/c changes.
Results (L/D = 1 table, linear interpolation in S):

Reading the table. A smaller clearance raises S, lowers ε and, in this heavily loaded range, gives a thicker film (8.4 μm against 6.7 μm). But it cuts the oil flow and raises friction a little, so the oil heats more (12.9 °C against 7.9 °C). A larger clearance runs cooler with more flow but more eccentric, and the film thins; it also tolerates less precision in manufacture. Very small clearances are hard to make and are upset by thermal growth and dirt.
Against the rule. The roughness rule asks for h₀ ≥ 0.007 mm at D = 50 mm. c = 0.06 mm fails (6.7 μm), c = 0.05 mm just passes (7.4 μm), c = 0.04 mm passes with margin (8.4 μm).

L/D. A longer bearing (larger L/D) lowers p for the same load, raises S and the film, but runs hotter and suffers from shaft slope at its ends; a shorter one leaks more oil and runs cooler but carries less. Values from about 0.5 to 1.5 are used, L/D = 1 being the usual compromise; each L/D needs its own curve.

Recommendation. For this steady load at moderate speed keep L/D = 1 and choose c = 0.04 mm (c/r = 0.0016, inside the usual 0.001 to 0.002), which gives the thickest film and a 12.9 °C rise that a 40 °C inlet easily absorbs. If the temperature is a worry, keep c = 0.05 mm and use a thicker oil to restore the margin.

bank.q: Design a full hydrodynamic journal bearing for a steady load of 20 kN at 1000 rpm. Take L/D = 1, an allowable bearing pressure of 2 MPa, clearance ratio c/r = 0.001, oil inlet 40 °C and an oil of μ = 0.025 Pa·s at the expected mean film temperature of 50 °C. Size the bearing, compute S, use the L/D = 1 table to find the film, friction, flow and temperature rise, and check the design.
outline: Size from p: L D = W/p
c from c/r
n in rev/s; S = (μn/p)(r/c)²
Interpolate ε, (r/c)f, Q/(rcnL), Q<sub>s</sub>/Q, p/p<sub>max</sub>
h₀, f, T, P<sub>f</sub>, Q, ΔT
Mean temperature against the assumed 50 °C
h₀ against the roughness rule; peak pressure

answer.text: Size. With L = D and p = 2 MPa: L D = D² = W/p = 20 000/2 = 10 000 mm², so D = 100 mm and L = 100 mm. Radius r = 50 mm.
Clearance. c/r = 0.001 gives c = 0.05 mm (diametral clearance 0.10 mm) and r/c = 1000.
Speed and pressure in SI: n = 1000/60 = 16.67 rev/s; p = 20 000/(0.1 × 0.1) = 2.0 × 10⁶ Pa.
Table rows that bracket S = 0.208 (L/D = 1):
Oil flow: Q = 4.122 × r c n L = 4.122 × 50 × 0.05 × 16.67 × 100 = 17 176 mm³/s = 17.2 cm³/s (about 1.03 litres a minute); side leakage Q<sub>s</sub> = 0.568 × 17 176 = 9760 mm³/s.
Temperature loop: mean film temperature = 40 + 19.3/2 = 49.6 °C, which matches the assumed 50 °C, so the viscosity used is right and no second pass is needed. Outlet oil 40 + 19.3 = 59.3 °C.
Checks:

Assumptions stated: full 360° bearing, steady load, aligned shaft, Newtonian oil, all friction heat carried by the oil flow (ρ = 860 kg/m³, c<sub>p</sub> = 1.76 kJ/(kg·K)), linear interpolation between table rows. Final design: D = L = 100 mm, c = 0.05 mm, oil of 0.025 Pa·s at 50 °C supplied at 40 °C and at least 17 cm³/s; the journal runs at ε ≈ 0.48 with a 26 μm film and loses about 0.5 kW.

glossary.def: A machine element that supports a moving part, carries its load and reduces friction between the moving and fixed surfaces.
The replaceable ring of bearing metal in which a journal turns or slides.
A soft white-metal lining alloy of tin or lead with antimony and copper, used on steel shells because it conforms to the shaft and embeds dirt.
The portion of a shaft that turns inside a bearing.
Half the difference between bush bore and journal diameter, the space available for the oil film when the shaft is centred.
The angle between the load direction and the line joining bush centre to shaft centre in a loaded journal bearing.
Load divided by the projected area, P = W/(L·d), used as the nominal pressure in bearing design.
A set of dimensionless design curves for full journal bearings giving eccentricity, film thickness, friction, oil flow and temperature rise against the Sommerfeld number for various L/D.
The commonest ball bearing, with raceway grooves that take radial load and either direction of axial load.
The life in millions of revolutions that a rolling bearing reaches or exceeds with 90% reliability under a stated load.
A multiplying factor applied to the L₁₀ life when a reliability other than 90% is required; it is below 1 for higher reliability.
A multiplier on the calculated load that allows for shock, vibration and duty of the driven machine.
The property of an oil that lets it cling to and lubricate surfaces under boundary conditions, separate from viscosity.
A chemical added to oil or grease that reacts with the metal under high contact pressure to form a low-shear surface film.
A standard number for an oil's kinematic viscosity at 40 °C, such as ISO VG 32 or VG 68, used to specify lubricants.
Any substance placed between sliding or rolling surfaces to keep them apart and reduce friction and wear.
A full fluid film supplied by an external pump at pressure, used where the speed is too low to build hydrodynamic pressure.
The ratio c/r of radial clearance to journal radius; it appears squared in the Sommerfeld number.
An unstable self-excited motion of a lightly loaded high-speed journal in which the shaft centre circles inside the bush.
A hardened ball, cylindrical roller, needle or tapered roller that separates the bearing rings with rolling rather than sliding contact.
L₁₀ in revolutions converted to running time, L<sub>10h</sub> = 10⁶ × L₁₀ ÷ (60 n) hours with n in rpm.
P₀ = X₀ F<sub>r</sub> + Y₀ F<sub>a</sub>, the load to compare against C₀ when the bearing is stationary or very slow.
Passages cut in the bush to distribute oil to the loaded zone; they are kept out of the load-carrying region so the film is not broken.
A compressible ring clamped between flanges to seal a static joint; it must be crushed to its seating stress before it seals.
The multiple of the fluid pressure that must stay on a gasket under pressure for the joint to stay tight.
An elastomer ring of round section squeezed in a groove; fluid pressure pushes it against the groove wall and tightens the seal.
A rubber lip held on a rotating shaft by a garter spring, facing the oil it holds back; the common gearbox and motor shaft seal.
A shaft seal in which a spring holds a rotating ring against a stationary ring, both lapped flat; used on pumps.
A non-contact seal of fins with small running gaps that throttle the leak; it never wears but always leaks a little.
